slides.title: A validation answers three questions, not one
slides.text: What validation must show A validation answers three questions, not one Conceptual soundness Is the design fit for the purpose: the target, the data, the features, the training choices? Outcome analysis Does it perform on rows it never saw: discrimination, calibration, intervals, every group? Monitoring Will anyone notice when it stops working: which metric, which threshold, who acts? This week. Day 1 and 2 are outcome analysis; Day 3 tests soundness of the explanations; Day 4 adds monitoring and the decision.

slides.title: Independent means other people, other rows and other questions
slides.text: Who validates Independent means other people, other rows and other questions The developers The validator Question Does my model work? Where does it stop working, and for whom? Rows Their training and test split Rows they never touched: calib and holdout Output A model and a card Rated findings, conditions of use, a decision At Mizan Rasil's credit analytics team Your model risk team, reporting to Dr. Sameera What goes wrong. A validator who retrains the model has become a second developer. Repairs are recommended, and the developers own them.

slides.title: Every claim gets one of three verdicts
slides.text: Reading a model card Every claim gets one of three verdicts Supported The package's evidence, or your recomputation, backs the claim as written. Unsupported The evidence is missing, or it contradicts the claim. Missing counts. Untestable No data you have, or could have today, can test it as written. Rewrite it as a test. The habit. "Supported" needs evidence. Silence is not support.

slides.title: Amana's card makes six claims
slides.text: The package you received Amana's card makes six claims It discriminates well: AUC 0.864 on a held-out sample of 4,000 applications. Its probabilities are well calibrated and can be read as default rates. It uses no gender, age or location information. Performance is consistent across all customer groups. It will remain accurate for the next three years. The reasons shown to officers are the causes of an applicant's risk. Also in the package. metadata.json (what they did) and evidence.json (what they measured). Read all three before computing anything.

slides.title: The claimed AUC came from rows the shipped model had seen
slides.text: One recomputation The claimed AUC came from rows the shipped model had seen Claimed in the card 0.864 On the training rows 0.858 On the holdout 0.755 The developers held out 4,000 rows, measured, then retrained on all rows and shipped that model. The shipped model has seen the 4,000 rows: its 0.864 is an in-sample number. On 10,000 rows it never saw: 0.755.

slides.title: Every guarantee this week holds under a condition you must state
slides.text: Guarantees and assumptions Every guarantee this week holds under a condition you must state Evidence It guarantees If this holds A holdout score Performance on similar new applicants New applicants look like the holdout Recalibration Average calibration The calib rows look like the applicants Conformal intervals 90% coverage on average Rows are exchangeable An explanation What the model does Not what causes default What goes wrong. A report that quotes the guarantee and drops the condition. The condition is where the next failure comes from.

slides.title: Validation data is applicants' personal data, even in a model risk team
slides.text: Responsible use Validation data is applicants' personal data, even in a model risk team Income, loans and missed payments of named people fall under the Personal Data Protection Law. A validator needs outcomes and predictions, not names: ask for the minimum, and ask the data protection officer. Subgroup columns (age band, gender, region) are needed to audit the model and must not leak into it. In this course Every applicant is synthetic. The capstone uses the course packages or a peer's synthetic package; no real borrower data enters a repository.

slides.title: Proper scores and reliability
slides.text: Session 2 Proper scores and reliability Compute the Brier score and log loss by hand and against a constant forecast Draw a reliability diagram from equal-count bins Explain why a model can rank well and still be miscalibrated 02

slides.title: A model can rank applicants well and still state the wrong risk
slides.text: Two different properties A model can rank applicants well and still state the wrong risk 0.755 AUC on the holdout: who is riskier than whom 0.40 mean predicted default probability, against 0.10 observed Discrimination : do defaulters get higher scores? AUC answers it, and ignores the scale. Calibration : when the model says 20%, do 20% default? AUC is blind to it. Officers read the score as a probability, so both matter.

slides.title: A proper score rewards the forecaster for saying what they believe
slides.text: Scoring a probability A proper score rewards the forecaster for saying what they believe def brier(y, p): return np.mean((p - y) ** 2) def log_loss(y, p): p = np.clip(p, 1e-12, 1 - 1e-12) return -np.mean(y * np.log(p) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - p)) Both are proper: the expected score is best when the forecast equals the true probability. Accuracy at 0.5 is not: 0.51 and 0.99 score the same. Log loss punishes a confident miss hard; Brier is bounded and easier to explain.

slides.title: As a probability, Amana loses to the base rate
slides.text: A forecast that knows nothing As a probability, Amana loses to the base rate Forecast on the holdout Brier Log loss AUC Amana, as shipped 0.199 0.586 0.755 Everyone gets the calib default rate 0.090 0.324 0.500 What goes wrong. Reporting AUC alone. The model that ranks better is the worse probability by both proper scores.

slides.title: A reliability diagram puts predicted against observed, bin by bin
slides.text: Seeing calibration A reliability diagram puts predicted against observed, bin by bin Bin (1,000 each) Predicted Observed Lowest 0.076 0.020 Fourth 0.262 0.042 Seventh 0.484 0.108 Highest 0.854 0.314 Sort by prediction, cut into equal-count bins, compare the means. Perfect calibration lies on the diagonal. Every Amana bin lies far below it. Expected calibration error: 0.30.

slides.title: Trained on a 50/50 sample, applied where one in ten defaults
slides.text: Why the curve is so low Trained on a 50/50 sample, applied where one in ten defaults 1 · Rebalance Non-defaults dropped until half the rows default → 2 · Train The model learns odds for a world with 50% defaults → 3 · Apply About 10% default: every probability is inflated A quick check. Rescaling the odds back to the true base rate brings the Brier score from 0.199 to 0.082. The proper repair is fitted on held-out rows: Session 3.

slides.title: Brier = reliability minus resolution plus uncertainty
slides.text: What the Brier score is made of Brier = reliability minus resolution plus uncertainty Reliability (miscalibration) 0.117 Uncertainty (the base rate) 0.089 Resolution (separation) 0.008 Read it. Amana loses more to miscalibration than it gains from separating applicants. Recalibration removes most of the first term and leaves the other two.

slides.title: Recalibration
slides.text: Session 3 Recalibration Fit Platt scaling and isotonic regression on a calibration split Score both on separate held-out rows, never on the rows that fitted them Choose a method and state what it cannot repair 03

slides.title: You calibrated your own model before; now you repair someone else's
slides.text: From DS-204 You calibrated your own model before; now you repair someone else's DS-204, Day 4 Calibration measured by decile on your own model, repaired on unseen rows, lost again under drift. Here Two maps compared with proper scores, the rows each may touch, what no map can repair, and the check by group.

slides.title: A recalibration map sits after the model and changes only the meaning of the score
slides.text: Recalibration A recalibration map sits after the model and changes only the meaning of the score Amana score, unchanged → Map fitted on the calib rows → Probability judged on the holdout The map is monotone, so the ranking and the AUC do not move. The developers can adopt it without retraining: it is a recommendation with evidence.

slides.title: Platt scaling fits one smooth curve; isotonic regression can step anywhere
slides.text: Two methods Platt scaling fits one smooth curve; isotonic regression can step anywhere Platt scaling A logistic regression of the outcome on the logit of the score: two parameters, a smooth S-shaped map. Steady with few rows. Isotonic regression Any non-decreasing step function of the score. Flexible, needs many rows, can overfit a small calib set. lr = LogisticRegression(C=1e6).fit(logit(p_cal).reshape(-1, 1), y_cal) platt = lambda q: lr.predict_proba(logit(q).reshape(-1, 1))[:, 1]

slides.title: Both maps cut the Brier score by more than half, and the AUC stays at 0.755
slides.text: Lab 1.3 on the holdout Both maps cut the Brier score by more than half, and the AUC stays at 0.755 Holdout Brier Log loss ECE AUC Raw Amana 0.199 0.586 0.304 0.755 Platt 0.081 0.284 0.011 0.755 Isotonic 0.081 0.287 0.012 0.754 Both now beat the base rate (Brier 0.090, log loss 0.324).

slides.title: A map judged on the rows that fitted it looks perfect
slides.text: What goes wrong A map judged on the rows that fitted it looks perfect 0.002 ECE of isotonic fitted and scored on the holdout 0.012 ECE of isotonic fitted on calib, scored on the holdout Isotonic regression can follow the noise of the rows it was fitted on. The honest error is six times larger. Same mistake as the claimed AUC of Lab 1.1, one step later.

slides.title: A map of the score cannot see what the score cannot see
slides.text: The limit of the repair A map of the score cannot see what the score cannot see It fixes the average relation between score and outcome. It cannot fix a group whose risk differs at the same score: a column the model never had. It cannot improve the ranking. It holds while new applicants resemble the calib rows; a shift breaks it again. Next session. Amana excludes region and age band on purpose. Is it calibrated within them?

slides.title: Calibrated on average can hide a group the model under-predicts
slides.text: Calibration by subgroup Calibrated on average can hide a group the model under-predicts After Platt, mean predicted 0.090 against 0.099 observed on the holdout. Region and age band are not features of Amana, by design. If risk differs between them at the same score, the average hides it. Why it matters at Mizan An under-predicted group gets loans priced below its risk; an over-predicted one is declined more than it should be. Both are harms to people.

slides.title: A gap in a group of 500 needs an interval before it is a finding
slides.text: Noise in small groups A gap in a group of 500 needs an interval before it is a finding def wilson(k, n, z=1.96): ph = k / n c = (ph + z*z/(2*n)) / (1 + z*z/n) h = z * np.sqrt(ph*(1-ph)/n + z*z/(4*n*n)) / (1 + z*z/n) return c - h, c + h The Northern region has 508 holdout applicants; 78 defaulted. The 95% Wilson interval for its rate: 12.5% to 18.8%. A finding is a prediction outside the interval, not any gap.

slides.title: Conformal intervals
slides.text: Session 1 Conformal intervals Compute the split conformal threshold with its finite-sample correction Wrap a fitted regression in intervals and check coverage on new rows State the one assumption the guarantee rests on 01

slides.title: A loss prediction of 12,000 riyals says nothing about how wrong it can be
slides.text: The problem A loss prediction of 12,000 riyals says nothing about how wrong it can be Amana's loss model predicts the riyals lost if a loan defaults. Finance provisions on it; collections plan on it. A point prediction is silent about its error: 12,000 could mean 11,000 to 13,000 or 2,000 to 30,000. What the validator adds An interval around every prediction that contains the real loss 90% of the time, with the condition under which that holds.

slides.title: Conformal prediction needs only one thing: new rows drawn like the calib rows
slides.text: The one assumption Conformal prediction needs only one thing: new rows drawn like the calib rows Exchangeable : the calib rows and the new row could be shuffled without changing their joint distribution. Independent draws from one population are exchangeable. No assumption on the model, the shape of the errors or the features. The guarantee breaks when the population moves: a new product, a new region, a shift in incomes. What goes wrong. Quoting "90% guaranteed" for applicants who no longer look like the calib rows. Session 4 measures how much is lost.

slides.title: Score the calib rows, take a quantile, widen every prediction by it
slides.text: Split conformal, in three steps Score the calib rows, take a quantile, widen every prediction by it 1 · Score On calib defaults, the error |loss - prediction| → 2 · Threshold The ceil((n+1)(1-α))-th smallest score → 3 · Interval prediction ± q, clipped at zero No retraining. The model is used as delivered; only its predictions on calib rows are needed.

slides.title: Counting the new loan turns "about 90%" into "at least 90%"
slides.text: Why "n + 1" Counting the new loan turns "about 90%" into "at least 90%" def conformal_quantile(scores, alpha=0.1): s = np.sort(scores) k = ceil((len(s) + 1) * (1 - alpha)) if k > len(s): return inf # too few rows return s[k - 1] The new loan's score is equally likely to fall at any of the n + 1 ranks. So the chance it falls at or below rank k is k / (n + 1), at least 90%. With 8 calib rows, 90% needs a ninth: the interval is infinite. Honest, and a warning about small groups.

MAPIE's SplitConformalRegressor with prefit=True returns the same half-width, 8,134.

slides.title: Coverage is a promise about the average over draws, not about one interval
slides.text: What the 90% promises Coverage is a promise about the average over draws, not about one interval 0.900 mean coverage over 100 random calib and test splits 0.867 to 0.935 the range across those splits One calib set can give 87% or 93% on one test set. "This loan has a 90% chance to fall in its interval" is not the promise. The promise is marginal: over loans and calib draws, on average.

slides.title: Prediction sets
slides.text: Session 2 Prediction sets Build LAC prediction sets from calibrated scores Build adaptive (APS) sets and compare their sizes Read a set of size one, two or three as a decision 02

slides.title: An officer who sees only the top grade cannot see the model's doubt
slides.text: Classification An officer who sees only the top grade cannot see the model's doubt Amana's grade model gives three probabilities: on time (A), late but repaid (B), default (C). The top grade is right for 74.4% of holdout applicants. For some it is a near-certainty; for others three grades are close. The top grade looks the same. A prediction set The grades the model cannot rule out, chosen so the true grade is in the set 90% of the time. Its size is the doubt.

slides.title: LAC keeps every grade whose probability clears one bar
slides.text: The simplest sets LAC keeps every grade whose probability clears one bar score = 1 - P_cal[i, true_grade] # calib rows q = conformal_quantile(score, 0.1) # 0.834 in_set = P_hold >= 1 - q # 0.166 Score: one minus the probability of the true grade. On Amana: a grade enters the set if its probability is at least 0.166. Smallest sets on average; can be empty.

slides.title: APS adds grades from most to least likely until their total reaches the threshold
slides.text: Adaptive sets APS adds grades from most to least likely until their total reaches the threshold Sort grades by probability → Accumulate add the next grade's probability → Stop when the total passes q (with a random share of the last grade) Unsure applicants, whose probabilities are spread, get larger sets. The randomisation makes coverage exact rather than conservative.

slides.title: When applicants change, the interval does not know
slides.text: Coverage under shift When applicants change, the interval does not know A conformal threshold is a fact about the calib rows. If next year's applicants earn more, borrow more or come from a new region, the rows are no longer exchangeable. The interval keeps its width and quietly loses coverage. At Mizan A planned campaign for salaried applicants with higher incomes. Higher incomes mean larger loans.

Strength 1: median declared income of defaulters from 9,400 to 16,100 riyals. The truth of every resampled row is known, so coverage can be measured exactly.

slides.title: PSI compares different applicants; a replay compares the same applicant twice
slides.text: Training and serving features PSI compares different applicants; a replay compares the same applicant twice Training path The job that built the training table, run again on the source records. Serving path The values the scoring service received and logged on the day. Drift: different applicants, different values; the two paths agree. Skew: the same applicant gets different values from the two paths. Replay: take scored applications, rebuild them through the training path, compare column by column with a tolerance fixed before looking.

slides.title: Before go-live, 200 replayed applications: the loan amount is 2% higher on every row

PSI of the served loan amount is 0.046, against 0.036 for the training values of the same rows. Yet 25 of 200 predictions rise by more than a point.

slides.title: The pattern of differences says which path to fix
slides.text: Reading a replay The pattern of differences says which path to fix Pattern Likely cause Action Every row, one constant ratio A unit or a definition in one path Fix that path, rescore Some rows, one category or source A code list, a join, a lookup Fix the mapping, rescore those rows Within tolerance only Different precision Nothing No row differs, the distribution moved The population changed Review the model, not the feed Fix the serving path. The training definition is the one the model learned.

slides.title: Name which applicants an officer must see, and give the officer the evidence
slides.text: Human review Name which applicants an officer must see, and give the officer the evidence A slogan "Borderline cases are reviewed by a human." A rule Every application from the Northern region, aged 18 to 24, or with all three grades in its 90% set. Automation Bias (guide p. 19): officers who see only a score defer to it. They need the grade set, stable reasons, authority to decide differently, and their overrides monitored.

slides.title: "Fit with conditions" is only as good as its owners and its monitoring
slides.text: Judgement "Fit with conditions" is only as good as its owners and its monitoring The model ranks well (AUC 0.755) and its probabilities are repaired: the harms found have conditions that remove them while causes are fixed. If no one will own C2 or C5, the honest decision is not fit. A condition without an owner is a wish; a review rule without a list of applicants is a slogan.
